Every curtailment number in the residual-load chapter that follows this
one is estimated — a curve fit to wind’s own potential-vs-observed gap,
transferred to PV under an assumption that’s never been checked against
real data. This chapter comes first for a reason: before trusting any
model of curtailment, it’s worth looking at real ground truth and building
a feel for how much of it there actually is, and when.

records.content:
Since July 2022, 

SMARD — the Bundesnetzagentur’s
electricity market data platform, already this project’s source for
generation and load — publishes monthly volumes of feed-in that was
adjusted under Germany’s Redispatch 2.0 congestion-management regime,
broken down by energy carrier (wind onshore, wind offshore, solar, and the
conventional sources). Two directions are published: reductions
(feed-in cut below what a plant could have produced — curtailment) and
increases (counter-trading up-regulation, plants asked to produce
more to compensate). Both are pulled by pecdr/smard_redispatch.py and
saved by pipeline/43_download_redispatch_by_source.py.

Unlike the rest of this project’s SMARD data, this series has no
documented API — the frontend multiplexes roughly 130 unrelated chart
series into one shared CSV, selected client-side by a chart_id column.
The download module re-derives the CSV’s current URL from the live


redispatch topic page
each run (rather than hardcoding it), since that URL is a CMS resource ID
that can change whenever the site is republished.

records.content:
It can: give real, technology-labeled, monthly curtailment volumes
covering July 2022 onward, at national scale. That’s enough to check
relative magnitudes between technologies and broad seasonal patterns.

It can’t: resolve anything at hourly or regional detail — there’s no
way to see which hour or which grid region drove a given month’s
number, so it can’t directly recalibrate the hourly oversupply-proxy curve
the residual-load model uses. It also only covers redispatch
(grid-operator-ordered curtailment) — market-based curtailment, where a
plant operator voluntarily cuts output because of negative prices, is a
separate mechanism entirely and doesn’t appear in this data at all. And it
starts in July 2022, so it can’t cover the earlier years of this project’s
2019-2025 backtest.

records.content:
Figure 1:Monthly redispatch curtailment (reduction) volume by energy source, July 2022 onward.

Wind — onshore and offshore together — dominates curtailment volume, and
both show a clear seasonal rhythm: more curtailment in the windier
autumn/winter months. PV’s curtailment is smaller in absolute terms but
just as clearly seasonal, tracking its own generation season instead.



Figure 2:Total curtailed energy per source over the full period.

The standout finding: wind offshore’s cumulative curtailment (16,108 GWh)
is actually larger than wind onshore’s (12,873 GWh), despite an
installed offshore fleet only about a seventh the size of onshore’s
(~9.2 GW vs. ~63.1 GW in 2025). Per MW installed, that’s roughly 8-9x
more curtailment for offshore than onshore — consistent with known
transmission bottlenecks moving generation from the northern coast to load
centers further south and west. This project’s residual-load model
currently pools onshore and offshore wind into a single curtailment curve
(notebooks 39/40/42) — this asymmetry is a real pattern that pooling
discards.



Figure 3:Average curtailment by calendar month, 2022-2026.

As a sanity check on the data’s own labeling: renewable sources sit at (or
extremely close to) 100% “reduction” share of their total redispatch
volume, while conventional/flexible sources (hard coal, gas, pumped
storage) split much more evenly between reductions and increases — exactly
what the reduction/increase terminology should imply if it means what it
says.

The wind-offshore workstream (see 

Wind offshore replication)
found a persistent positive bias against SMARD’s actual generation that
survives fixing capacity accounting (notebook 35) and correlates cleanly
with system-wide renewable oversupply (notebook 36) — evidence for
curtailment, but not proof, and not yet separated from the other candidate
explanations (outages, model error) or connected to the solar
workstream’s own open self-consumption question (26’s takeaways: bias
and self-consumption share grow together over time, “can’t separate...
from these two panels alone”). The wider project goal is a day-ahead
residual-load forecast, which needs two things that are never directly
observed: potential renewable generation net of curtailment, and gross
(not just grid-metered) power demand.

This page fixes notation once, then writes down every equation relating
potential generation, hidden losses, what’s actually observed, demand, and
storage — as a single reference for what’s being estimated, from what,
and why.

records.content:
1. Per-technology physical balance. What potential generation decomposes into: real-world losses plus whatever was actually produced, plus this project’s own model error.P_i(t) = L_{repair,i}(t) + L_{price,i}(t) + L_{congestion,i}(t) + Produced_i(t) + \varepsilon_i(t)

2. The produced/behind-the-meter split. What’s physically produced either reaches the public grid or is used behind the meter.Produced_i(t) = G_i(t) + BTM_i(t)

For wind, BTM_i(t) ≈ 0 structurally — this is what made the offshore
bias-driver analysis (notebook 36) a clean read on curtailment specifically,
with no self-consumption confound to separate out.

3. Behind-the-meter self-consumption, with battery time-shifting (PV only). Same-hour self-use plus whatever a paired battery discharges, minus whatever it charges.BTM_{pv}(t) = SelfUse_{pv}(t) + Discharge_{btm}(t) - Charge_{btm}(t)

4. Behind-the-meter battery state. The battery’s own stock-flow recursion — this is what turns self-consumption from a same-hour cancellation into a time-shifted one.SOC_{btm}(t) = SOC_{btm}(t-1) + Charge_{btm}(t) - Discharge_{btm}(t) - loss_{btm}(t)

5. System balance. An accounting identity, true by construction — not something to estimate. Whatever the grid draws must equal everything injected into it.D_{grid}(t) = \sum_i G_i(t) + \big(G_{storage,discharge}(t) - G_{storage,charge}(t)\big) + G_{other}(t) + NetImport(t)

6. Gross demand. Grid-metered load plus the invisible behind-the-meter piece.D_{true}(t) = D_{grid}(t) + D_{btm}(t)

D_btm(t) is met by BTM_i(t) first (mostly PV); any shortfall is drawn
from the grid (already inside D_grid); any BTM surplus beyond local
demand is either exported (counted in G_i) or wasted.

7. The gross-demand regression. This is the estimable link between the hidden demand side and what’s observed: grid-metered load equals a calendar/weather-driven demand model minus PV self-consumption, plus noise. Linear in every unknown, solvable with plain OLS — nighttime and heavily overcast hours (P_pv(t)≈0) pin down the demand-model coefficients with no self-consumption interference at all, since the -k·P_pv(t) term vanishes there; daytime hours (where P_pv(t) varies a lot at fixed calendar/weather conditions, due to cloud cover) then pin down k.D_{grid}(t) = \underbrace{\beta_0 + \beta_{dow}(t) + \beta_{holiday}\!\cdot\!Holiday(t) + f_{temp}(T(t)) + trend(t)}_{\hat D_{true}(t;\theta)} \; - \; k \cdot P_{pv}(t) + \varepsilon(t)

7a. Refinement: split by feed-in category. solar_capacity_by_pv_category_month already tracks which capacity is registered full_feed_in (required to export 100%, no self-consumption possible) versus self-consumption categories. Fitting separate coefficients gives a built-in falsification test.D_{grid}(t) = \hat D_{true}(t;\theta) - k_{full\_feed\_in} \cdot P_{pv,full\_feed\_in}(t) - k_{self\_consumption} \cdot P_{pv,self\_consumption}(t) + \varepsilon(t)

k_full_feed_in should come out statistically indistinguishable from zero; if it doesn’t, that’s a sign of a modeling problem, not a real effect. (A further, not-yet-formalized refinement: self-consumption should saturate — a household can’t self-consume more than its own local demand — so a piecewise-linear or spline term in P_pv(t) is more physically honest than a single linear k, and still OLS-solvable.)

8. The naive oversupply proxy (what notebooks 22/36 actually used), and why it’s biased. Built entirely from observed values — which is exactly the problem, since at the hours with the most curtailment, the observed numerator is already suppressed by that same curtailment.OversupplyProxy_{obs}(t) = \frac{G_{wind\_on}(t) + G_{wind\_off}(t) + G_{pv}(t)}{D_{grid}(t)}

9. The corrected, potential-based oversupply proxy. Curtailment decisions respond to the true oversupply situation, not the already-curtailed observed one — so the proxy driving L̂ should be built from potential and gross demand instead.OversupplyProxy_{potential}(t) = \frac{P_{total}(t)}{\hat D_{true}(t)}

10. The curtailment model, calibrated on wind and extrapolated to PV. Wind’s own gap has no BTM term to separate out, so it’s a clean training signal for how curtailment responds to oversupply; applying that same fitted relationship to PV’s own oversupply hours predicts PV’s curtailment without needing to observe it directly.Gap_{wind,i}(t) \approx L_{repair,i}(t) + L_{price,i}(t) + L_{congestion,i}(t) + \varepsilon_i(t), \qquad \hat L(t) = \hat L\big(OversupplyProxy_{potential}(t)\big)

10a. The residual left over for PV, once curtailment is subtracted out. Whatever remains of PV’s own gap after removing the wind-calibrated curtailment prediction is an estimate of PV’s self-consumption plus its own repair losses and model error.Gap_{pv}(t) - \hat L_{pv}(t) \;\approx\; BTM_{pv}(t) + L_{repair,pv}(t) + \varepsilon_{pv}(t)

Cross-checkable against solar_capacity_by_pv_category_month: if this
residual tracks the self-consumption-registered capacity share over time,
that’s independent corroboration it’s really BTM, not ε or
L_repair. L_repair and ε stay bundled throughout this whole chain —
genuinely unidentifiable further without real outage data or an
independently validated model, neither of which this project has.

11. The forecasting target. Realized residual load is a pure accounting identity from already-observed values — nothing to estimate. The forecastable version substitutes gross demand and potential-minus-estimated-curtailment for the observed quantities, so it can be computed ahead of time from weather and calendar alone.ResidualLoad(t) = D_{grid}(t) - \sum_i G_i(t)\widehat{ResidualLoad}(t) = \hat D_{true}(t) - \big(P_{total}(t) - \hat L(t)\big)

Note that BTM doesn’t appear in the forecast formula at all — it cancels
out of residual load exactly as it does in the realized version (the
self-consumed MWh is absent from both published generation and published
demand equally). It still earned its place in equation 7: without the
-k·P_pv(t) term, D̂_true(t) itself would be biased by mistaking the
solar self-consumption dip for a real demand pattern. BTM matters for
getting the demand model right; it drops out of the final target.

An earlier idea was to use realized fossil generation + net imports as a
third, BTM-free channel to estimate L_price + L_congestion for the whole
system independently of the per-technology gaps. Writing the system
balance out at both potential and actual renewable output kills this:Gap_{total}(t) \equiv \sum_i \big(P_i(t) - G_i(t)\big)
= \big(D_{grid}(t) - \textstyle\sum_i P_i(t)\big) - \big(D_{grid}(t) - \sum_i G_i(t)\big)

which reduces to Gap_total(t) = Gap_total(t) — tautological. Without an
actual dispatch/merit-order model, “counterfactual fossil+import” is defined
as whatever the residual demands, so it adds no information beyond P and
G directly. Fossil/import data isn’t worthless — it can show whether
must-run constraints are binding (fossil pinned at a floor, forcing
curtailment as the only release valve) — but that’s mechanism evidence,
not a new decomposition axis, and shouldn’t be oversold as one.

Checked directly by building a download pipeline against it, not just
assumed: SMARD publishes monthly redispatch-adjusted feed-in volumes by
energy carrier (wind onshore, wind offshore, solar, and the conventional
sources), covering July 2022 onward — see


the congestion data chapter for the full
walkthrough and pecdr/smard_redispatch.py/pipeline/43_download_redispatch_by_source.py
for how it’s fetched. That’s real ground truth for L_congestion
specifically, per technology, but with real limits: (1) it starts July
2022, so it can’t cover this project’s full 2019-2025 backtest; (2) it’s
monthly and national-only — no hour-of-day or grid-region detail, so
it can’t directly recalibrate an hourly oversupply-proxy curve the way a
per-measure, per-plant series could; (3) it only captures redispatch
(grid-operator-ordered curtailment) — it never captures L_price
(voluntary, market-based curtailment from negative prices) or L_repair
(not a redispatch measure at all).

(An earlier version of this section described 

netztransparenz.de’s
per-measure Redispatch export, assumed to carry a clean per-technology
breakdown from October 2021 — that assumption was never actually verified
and turned out not to hold up on inspection; SMARD’s own monthly series,
above, is the source this project actually downloads and uses.)

Because tomorrow’s curtailment is never observable at forecast time
regardless, L̂(t) in equation 11 has to be an estimated function of
forecastable inputs either way — real congestion data’s role is
validating or recalibrating that estimated function against history,
not supplying it a live input. The one thing this monthly data already
makes checkable: it shows wind offshore curtailed roughly 8-9x more
heavily per MW installed than onshore (see the congestion data chapter) —
a real technology-specific asymmetry that the pooled onshore+offshore
curtailment curve in notebooks 39/40/42 currently discards.

This chapter is self-contained: every symbol is defined where it first
appears, and nothing here depends on having read anything else in this
book. It builds up, step by step, one growing diagram of how Germany’s
electricity system fits together — starting from the one number everyone
already has an intuition for (how much power the grid delivers) and
ending at the quantity this project actually wants to forecast:
residual load, the part of demand that has to be met by dispatchable
generation once weather-driven renewables have done what they can.

The notation matches pecdr/residual_load.py and the more exhaustive


equations reference page one-for-one,
so nothing has to be relearned if you already know those — but nothing
here assumes you do. Where this chapter simplifies or omits something
the reference page covers in full (behind-the-meter battery dynamics,
the feed-in-category split, a dead-end derivation worth knowing about),
it says so and points there.

Start with the one quantity that’s simply measured, not estimated: D_grid(t), SMARD’s published grid load at hour t — how much power was drawn from the German public grid. Every megawatt of it has to come from somewhere: wind onshore, wind offshore, solar PV, or everything else (hydro, fossil, biomass, nuclear until 2023, geothermal — grouped here as G_other(t), since this project doesn’t model a weather-driven “potential” for any of it), plus whatever crosses the border.D_{grid}(t) = G_{wind\_on}(t) + G_{wind\_off}(t) + G_{pv}(t) + G_{other}(t) + \big(G_{storage,discharge}(t) - G_{storage,charge}(t)\big) + NetImport(t)flowchart LR Gwo["G_wind_on(t)"] --> Sum(("Σ")) Gwf["G_wind_off(t)"] --> Sum Gpv["G_pv(t)"] --> Sum Goth["G_other(t)
hydro, fossil, biomass, nuclear, ..."] --> Sum Stor["storage net
(mention only — not modeled below)"] -.-> Sum Imp["NetImport(t)
+ = net importing, − = net exporting"] --> Sum Sum --> Dgrid["D_grid(t)
SMARD's published load"] This is an accounting identity, true by construction — nothing here is estimated or forecast, it’s just bookkeeping. It also settles a question that’s easy to get tangled in: does exporting power count as part of “demand”? No — NetImport(t) is signed. When Germany is a net exporter, NetImport(t) < 0, and the identity says domestic generation has to cover both D_grid(t) and the amount leaving the country. Export doesn’t split D_grid(t)'s stacked bar; it sits on the generation side of the same balance, as a negative import. Grid-scale storage (pumped hydro, increasingly grid batteries) is real and already in this identity, but genuinely just mentioned here — not pulled into anything that follows.

Of the terms in Step 1’s identity, three are weather-driven and variable: wind onshore, wind offshore, and PV. Their output depends on what the weather happens to be doing, not on a dispatch decision. Everything in G_other(t) — plus imports — is treated in this project as dispatchable: available more or less on demand, within its own constraints, and (for domestic fossil generation specifically) what actually sets the price in a merit-order market. Residual load is defined as what’s left of grid demand once those three weather-driven technologies are subtracted:ResidualLoad(t) = D_{grid}(t) - \big(G_{wind\_on}(t) + G_{wind\_off}(t) + G_{pv}(t)\big)flowchart LR subgraph Weather["weather-driven, subtracted for residual load"] Gwo["G_wind_on(t)"] Gwf["G_wind_off(t)"] Gpv["G_pv(t)"] end Goth["G_other(t) + NetImport(t)
+ storage net"] Weather --> Dgrid["D_grid(t)"] Goth --> Dgrid Dgrid --> RL["ResidualLoad(t)
= D_grid(t) − ΣG_i(t)
i ∈ {wind_on, wind_off, pv}"] Weather -.->|subtracted| RL This is a scope decision worth naming, not hiding. Hydro is partly weather-driven too (run-of-river especially), and PECD does publish hydro capacity factors — this project just doesn’t currently model hydro potential or subtract it here. It’s grouped into G_other(t) alongside genuinely dispatchable fossil and biomass generation. That’s a reasonable simplification (German hydro is a small share of the mix, and much of it — reservoir and pumped storage — really is dispatchable), but it means “residual load” here is narrower than “load minus all renewables”; it’s specifically “load minus the two technologies this project models a weather-driven potential for.”

records.content:
D_grid(t) and every G_i(t) above are net of something neither side publishes: behind-the-meter (BTM) self-consumption — power generated and used locally, never touching the public grid. It’s asymmetric across technologies: Germany’s wind fleet is essentially 100% utility-scale and always grid-connected, so BTM_{wind\_on}(t) ≈ BTM_{wind\_off}(t) ≈ 0 structurally. PV is different — MaStR (Germany’s public plant register) splits PV capacity into a full_feed_in category (required to export 100%, no self-consumption possible by regulation) and self-consumption categories, and BTM is concentrated in the latter — measured from the registry, not assumed, and it skews toward smaller rooftop installations rather than utility-scale plants. What’s physically produced splits into what reaches the grid and what’s used behind the meter:Produced_i(t) = G_i(t) + BTM_i(t) And on the demand side, the mirror image: grid-metered demand plus the invisible BTM demand met by local self-consumption is gross demand, never directly observed:D_{true}(t) = D_{grid}(t) + D_{btm}(t) (BTM_pv(t) can also be time-shifted through a paired rooftop battery — same-hour self-use plus battery discharge minus battery charge, with its own state-of-charge recursion. Real, and mentioned for completeness, but not modeled anywhere below; see the equations reference page for the full battery notation if needed.) Putting the whole thing together — potential generation splitting into losses (next step) and what’s produced, produced splitting into grid and behind-the-meter, and D_grid(t) (from Step 1’s balance) sitting alongside gross demand:flowchart TD P["Potential generation
P_i(t), i ∈ {wind_on, wind_off, pv}"] -->|"− L_repair,i(t) − L_price,i(t) − L_congestion,i(t) − ε_i(t)"| Produced["Produced_i(t)"] Produced -->|grid-injected| G["G_i(t)
observed, SMARD"] Produced -->|"self-consumed, PV only
BTM_i(t)"| BTM["Behind-the-meter
generation"] G --> Dgrid["D_grid(t)"] Goth["G_other(t) + NetImport(t)
+ storage net"] --> Dgrid Dgrid --> RL["ResidualLoad(t)
= D_grid(t) − ΣG_i(t)"] Dgrid --> Dtrue["D_true(t)
= D_grid(t) + D_btm(t)"] BTM --> Dtrue This is the full structural picture the rest of this chapter fills in. Read it left to right: potential splits into loss streams and what’s actually produced; produced splits again into grid-injected and behind-the-meter; the behind-the-meter piece reappears on the demand side, combining with D_grid(t) into gross demand D_true(t). ResidualLoad(t) only ever touches the grid boxes — which is exactly why BTM turns out to cancel out of it (Step 9), even though it still has to be modeled correctly to get D_true(t) right along the way (Step 6).

records.content:
Everything in the diagram above except P_i(t), the loss terms, BTM,
and D_true(t) is something SMARD already publishes. ResidualLoad(t)
itself can be computed today, directly, from already-published numbers —
no modeling needed, just Step 2’s subtraction.

The reason to go further is that the actual goal is a day-ahead
forecast of residual load — tomorrow’s number, before SMARD has
published anything for tomorrow. And the already-published quantities
are exactly the ones you can’t forecast directly from weather and
calendar, because they’re already contaminated by things that haven’t
happened yet from a forecaster’s point of view: G_i(t) is already net
of curtailment nobody has decided on yet, and D_grid(t) is already net
of self-consumption that depends on tomorrow’s cloud cover. What
can be forecast from weather and calendar are the underlying physical
and behavioral quantities: P_i(t) (what the fleet would produce, given
a weather forecast) and D_true(t) (what people and industry actually
want to consume, given a calendar and a temperature forecast). The next
few steps build both.

records.content:
P_i(t) is this project’s own modeled, weather-driven technical
potential for technology i ∈ {wind_on, wind_off, pv} — what the
installed fleet would generate given the weather, before any real-world
loss. It’s built from ERA5 reanalysis weather (bias-corrected against the
Global Wind Atlas for wind, extrapolated to each turbine’s hub height)
and MaStR’s own record of which plants exist, where, and of what type —
the same replication effort documented in this book’s wind and solar
workstreams, cross-checked against PECD’s own published capacity factors
at every step. P_total(t) = P_{wind\_on}(t) + P_{wind\_off}(t) + P_{pv}(t).

Potential splits into real-world losses plus whatever’s actually
produced (plus this project’s own model error, kept separate on
principle even though it’s empirically indistinguishable from real
losses without independent validation):P_i(t) = L_{repair,i}(t) + L_{price,i}(t) + L_{congestion,i}(t) + Produced_i(t) + \varepsilon_i(t)

L_repair,i(t) — technical unavailability: storm damage, cable
faults, scheduled maintenance. Independent of price or grid signals.

L_price,i(t) — voluntary curtailment during negative prices. Not
a grid-operator order, and not in any published redispatch dataset.

L_congestion,i(t) — grid-operator-enforced curtailment
(Redispatch 2.0 / Einspeisemanagement). The one loss category with
published official data — but only from October 2021, and even then
only monthly and national-only (see the


congestion data chapter for what
that data does and doesn’t cover).

Looking at the gap between potential and observed generation directly is
the first evidence this isn’t just bookkeeping:



Figure 1:Wind offshore, Nov-Dec 2023: potential vs. observed (SMARD). No behind-the-meter term to blur the picture, so this gap is (almost) entirely loss.



Figure 2:Solar PV, Jun-Jul 2023: potential vs. observed (SMARD). A gap at every peak, not just high-oversupply days — consistent with self-consumption (constant) layered on top of curtailment (episodic).

Wind’s gap is (almost) pure loss, since BTM_{wind}(t) ≈ 0 — that’s
what makes it the clean calibration signal used in Step 8. PV’s gap
mixes loss and self-consumption together; separating them needs Step 6
and Step 8 both.

records.content:
The estimable link between the hidden demand side and what SMARD
publishes: grid-metered load equals a calendar/temperature demand model,
minus PV self-consumption, plus noise.D_{grid}(t) = \underbrace{\beta_0 + \beta_{dow}(t) + \beta_{holiday}\!\cdot\!Holiday(t) + f_{temp}(T(t)) + trend(t)}_{\hat D_{true}(t;\theta)} \; - \; k \cdot P_{pv}(t) + \varepsilon(t)

The predictors actually used: day-of-week (dow(t)), hour-of-day (as a
categorical, alongside dow), a German public-holiday indicator
(Holiday(t)), heating- and cooling-degree terms built from area-average
German temperature (T(t)), and a slow linear trend (trend(t)) for
structural change over 2019-2025 (e.g. 2022’s demand destruction from the
energy-price crisis).

Two honest gaps worth flagging rather than glossing over: temperature
is area-average, not population-weighted — PECD does publish a
population-weighted temperature product, but only at the pan-European
synchronous-zone level, which can’t isolate Germany specifically, so
area-average is what’s used instead. And there’s no explicit
day-of-year / seasonal term beyond what temperature already captures —
if there’s a seasonal demand pattern that isn’t just “hot” or “cold”
(daylight-driven behavior, industrial calendars), the current model
doesn’t have a dedicated term for it.

Why this regression is identifiable at all: P_pv(t) ≈ 0 at night
and on heavily overcast days, so the -k·P_pv(t) term vanishes there —
nighttime and overcast hours pin down θ (the calendar/temperature
coefficients) with zero self-consumption interference. Daytime hours,
where P_pv(t) varies a lot from cloud cover at otherwise-fixed
calendar/weather conditions, then pin down k. One regression, not two
sequential models.

The fitted self-consumption share comes out around 12% of national PV
potential, net of the ~40% of the fleet registered full_feed_in
(structurally excluded from self-consumption by regulation). Two
built-in falsification checks were run and both came back non-zero
rather than the expected zero — investigated rather than dismissed: the
full_feed_in category’s own coefficient should be indistinguishable
from zero but isn’t, because its regressor correlates at 0.95 with the
one that should show an effect, leaving too little independent
variation for OLS to separate them; and wind potential (no
self-consumption channel at all) also came back significant, surviving a
direct test of the obvious alternative (a much richer temperature
response barely changed it) — more likely a real, different phenomenon:
price-responsive industrial demand rising during cheap, high-wind hours.
Full detail in the 

walkthrough.

records.content:
To predict curtailment from an oversupply signal, that signal has to be
built from things curtailment hasn’t already touched. The naive version
isn’t:OversupplyProxy_{obs}(t) = \frac{G_{wind\_on}(t) + G_{wind\_off}(t) + G_{pv}(t)}{D_{grid}(t)}

— built from already-curtailed observed generation, so it understates
true oversupply exactly when curtailment is largest. The corrected
version swaps in potential generation and estimated gross demand
instead:OversupplyProxy_{potential}(t) = \frac{P_{total}(t)}{\hat D_{true}(t)}

records.content:
Gap_i(t) = P_i(t) - G_i(t) is directly computable from what’s already
built. On wind, this gap is (almost) pure loss (Step 5) — a clean
training signal for how curtailment responds to oversupply:Gap_{wind,i}(t) \approx L_{repair,i}(t) + L_{price,i}(t) + L_{congestion,i}(t) + \varepsilon_i(t), \qquad \hat L(t) = \hat L\big(OversupplyProxy_{potential}(t)\big)

fit as an empirical bin-mean curtailment rate vs. oversupply, not an
assumed functional form. Applying that same fitted curve to PV’s own
oversupply hours, via PV’s own potential, predicts PV’s curtailment
without needing to observe it directly — and whatever’s left of PV’s gap
after subtracting it is an estimate of self-consumption plus PV’s own
repair loss:Gap_{pv}(t) - \hat L_{pv}(t) \;\approx\; BTM_{pv}(t) + L_{repair,pv}(t) + \varepsilon_{pv}(t)



Figure 3:PV’s average gap against SMARD, decomposed into predicted curtailment vs. the self-consumption-plus-repair remainder.

The headline surprise: curtailment, not self-consumption, is the
larger piece of PV’s own gap (76%) — not obvious going in, since
self-consumption is the effect that usually gets talked about.

Two checks worth knowing about: onshore and offshore wind’s own
curtailment-vs-oversupply curves (both BTM-free) agree from moderate
oversupply upward — the range that matters for PV’s daylight hours,
supporting the one-shared-curve transfer. And the leftover PV residual
above correlates at 0.643 with an independent series the model never
sees during fitting (MaStR’s self-consumption-registered capacity
share) — supportive, though both simply trend upward together over
2019-2025, so treat it as suggestive rather than tightly validated.

Real redispatch data (SMARD, monthly, from July 2022) shows offshore
wind curtailed roughly 8-9x more heavily per MW installed than
onshore — a real technology-specific asymmetry the pooled onshore+offshore
curve above currently discards (see the


congestion data chapter for the full
picture; that data validates an already-fitted curve after the fact, it
can’t supply \hat L(t) a live forecasting input, since tomorrow’s
curtailment is never observable at forecast time regardless of what data
exists).

records.content:
Realized residual load is a pure accounting identity — Step 2’s
subtraction, nothing to estimate:ResidualLoad(t) = D_{grid}(t) - \sum_i G_i(t)

The forecastable version substitutes gross demand and
potential-minus-estimated-curtailment for the observed quantities, so it
can be computed ahead of time from weather and calendar alone:\widehat{ResidualLoad}(t) = \hat D_{true}(t) - \big(P_{total}(t) - \hat L(t)\big)

Note BTM doesn’t appear here at all — it cancels out exactly as it
does in the realized version, since the self-consumed MWh is absent from
both published generation and published demand in equal measure. It
still earned its place in Step 6: without the -k·P_pv(t) term,
\hat D_{true}(t) itself would mistake the self-consumption dip for a
real demand pattern.

Roughly half the MAE, a quarter of the bias — but a humbling result
alongside it, worth stating plainly rather than only celebrating the
win: a plain linear regression given the same inputs as the full
structural model above, with none of its hand-built equations, does
slightly better on this same backtest (MAE 4,177 MW, corr 0.941).



Figure 5:Out-of-time MAE across six models — calendar-only, naive, this chapter’s full structural model, a plain linear regression on the same features, and two LightGBM variants.

Most of the benefit in this backtest comes from having the right
features at all (weather-derived potential, corrected for curtailment
in some form) rather than from the specific structural extraction of
D_true and the curtailment curve. That doesn’t make the structure
wasted — it’s what makes the falsification checks, the wind/PV
decomposition, and this chapter’s account of why the gap exists
possible, none of which a flat regression offers — but as a pure
point-forecast, it needed to earn its keep here and, on this specific
test, didn’t quite. Full six-model detail in the


walkthrough.

records.content:
Germany’s day-ahead auction clears on a pre-redispatch basis — the
price is set before grid operators intervene to relieve congestion.
SMARD’s published generation, by contrast, is post-redispatch — it’s
already had L_congestion applied. Every G_i(t) used throughout this
chapter, and therefore ResidualLoad(t) and the \hat L(t) fit against
it, is a post-redispatch quantity.

That’s fine for forecasting what actually reaches the grid. It’s a
real problem if the eventual target shifts to forecasting the
day-ahead price specifically: a price-relevant residual load should
only net out L_repair and L_price — the losses that exist before
the auction clears — not L_congestion, which happens after. But \hat L(t) in Step 8 is fit on wind’s total gap, because hourly
per-loss-type data doesn’t exist (Step 8’s redispatch data is monthly
and national-only). There’s currently no way to strip L_congestion
back out of \hat L(t) to build that narrower, price-relevant target.
Flagged here explicitly as unresolved, not swept into the roadmap below
as if it were just more of the same work.

records.content:
If potential (P_i(t)), curtailment (\hat L(t)), and gross demand
(\hat D_{true}(t)) can each be reconstructed well against historical
weather, the same pipeline should run forward: feed it a weather
forecast instead of realized weather, and \widehat{ResidualLoad}(t)
for tomorrow falls out directly, without ever needing tomorrow’s
curtailment or self-consumption to be observed. One caveat that belongs
here, not in a footnote: every backtest number in Step 9 uses realized
historical weather, not a forecast — it measures how well known weather
translates into residual load, not genuine multi-day-ahead forecast
skill. A real 5-15-day deployment would feed this same pipeline actual
NWP forecast fields, and forecast error (especially wind-speed timing
beyond a few days) stacks on top of everything measured here.

If the target moves from grid-injected residual load to day-ahead
price, Step 10’s tension has to be resolved first — most likely by
finding a way to separate L_congestion from L_price + L_repair
rather than treating \hat L(t) as one bundled curve, or by explicitly
quantifying how much error the current bundled target introduces when
used as a price proxy.

All three workstreams are checked the same way in the end: weight a modeled
capacity factor up to a national figure using MaStR’s own time-varying
installed capacity, then compare against SMARD’s actual net generation
over the full 2019-2025 backtest (61,368 hours). Three points of
comparison throughout: PECD’s own official product (reweighted by MaStR
capacity, not a replication at all — the best available anchor for “how
good can this possibly get”), the simplest from-scratch physics baseline
this project started from, and this project’s own best replication.

Workstream

PECD official × MaStR

Naive physics baseline

This project’s own replication

Wind onshore

MAE 0.029, corr 0.985

MAE 0.089, corr 0.931

MAE 0.065, corr 0.983

Wind offshore

MAE 0.094, corr 0.902

MAE 0.133, corr 0.882

MAE 0.128, corr 0.916

Solar PV

MAE 0.016, corr 0.981

Wind is essentially converged: this project’s full replication
(GWA bias-adjusted wind speed, alpha hub-height extrapolation, per-plant
power curves) reaches corr 0.983 against real SMARD generation — a hair
under PECD’s own 0.985, and far past the naive baseline’s 0.931. The
remaining open item is a systematic high-wind over-estimate, most likely
from the wake-effect/farm-layout modeling this project deliberately
doesn’t attempt (see the roadmap below).

Wind offshore reaches the best correlation of the three (0.916), but a
larger bias than either other approach: the same per-plant chain as
onshore, adapted for two offshore-specific findings (GWA2’s
bias-correction reference barely reaches past ~20km offshore; the shared
storm-shutdown model over-derates in wind speeds offshore sees regularly
but onshore rarely does — see the section below). The replication’s
correlation edges out even PECD’s own official product (0.916 vs. 0.902),
but its bias (+0.108) is about 50% larger than PECD’s own (+0.073) and the
naive baseline’s (+0.071), which now come out statistically close to each
other — against real SMARD generation, most likely unmodeled offshore
curtailment from delayed grid
connections, a well-documented real-world issue neither model attempts.

Solar has closed much of the gap but not all of it: swapping in
PECD’s fully documented PV conversion chain (Skartveit-Olseth
decomposition, Klucher transposition, Martin-Ruiz optical losses, a Beyer
et al. efficiency polynomial, Ross cell temperature, real per-plant
orientation from MaStR) took correlation against SMARD from 0.926 to
0.937 and MAE from 0.057 to 0.046 — a real, year-over-year-consistent
improvement over the naive baseline. But PECD’s own product is still
roughly 3x closer to reality (MAE 0.016 vs. 0.046) than this project’s
best replication gets. Open candidates, none conclusively resolved yet:

PECD’s documented inverter-loss polynomial (Schmidt & Sauer, 1994):
applying it exactly as written makes the match against PECD’s own

instead (

around +0.08-0.09 capacity-factor bias above ~30% output — consistent

product — get measurably worse year over year, 2019 through 2025.

share, unmodeled panel degradation, or a shifting technology mix
(

records.content:
If we know the weather and which power plants exist, we can, in principle,
compute power output directly from physical equations — no statistical
model needed. Suppose demand were fully price-inelastic (fixed regardless
of price). Then total generation must equal demand at every instant. If
renewables generate less than is demanded, the gap — the residual
load — has to be met by something else: coal or gas plants domestically,
or imports (nuclear power from a neighboring country, for instance).

Residual load is, by definition, just demand minus renewable generation. So
if we can forecast renewable generation well, we get residual load for free
— which is arguably the more economically interesting quantity, since it’s
residual load that drives prices, dispatch, and import/export flows.

records.content:
Even where the physical equations themselves are well understood (wind is
the clearest example), several things stand between “we know the weather”
and “we know the exact power injected into the grid”:

High-wind shutdown. Turbines cut out above some wind speed for
safety. Modelable in principle from wind speed alone, but PECD’s own
methodology treats it as a per-turbine hysteresis process (shutdown and
restart at different thresholds), which needs state we don’t have.

Wind farm layout and wake effects. Where exactly a turbine sits
inside its farm, and which direction the wind is blowing from, changes
what wind speed it actually experiences — a front-row turbine sees
different wind than one further back, whose approaching wind has
already been slowed and turbulized by the rows ahead of it.

Outages. Wind farms are sometimes offline entirely for maintenance
or repair, independent of weather.

Curtailment. When the grid is congested, some turbines aren’t
allowed to feed in at all, regardless of how much wind is available.
This is expected to become more common, not less, as renewable
penetration grows.

No ground truth for any of the above, individually. There is no
published time series that isolates “generation lost to curtailment” or
“generation lost to an outage” — only the net result reaches public
data.

The behind-the-meter blind spot. Grid statistics (SMARD, in this
project’s case) only observe power in front of the meter — what
actually crosses into the public grid. Anything happening behind the
meter is invisible: if someone generates electricity and consumes it
themselves, it shows up in neither the published generation figure nor
the published demand figure. What we actually have access to is net
generation and net demand, both already reduced by whatever
self-consumption happened behind meters we can’t see.

This has a subtle consequence for residual load specifically: since
self-consumption is missing from both sides of the residual-load
calculation in equal measure (the self-consumed MWh is absent from
published generation, but also absent from published demand, since it
was never drawn from the grid), the two omissions cancel and residual
load itself stays largely correct. What breaks is any direct comparison
of our own gross physical generation estimate against SMARD’s
net generation figure — that comparison is not apples-to-apples
unless self-consumption is explicitly accounted for.

To compute gross wind production for a given weather situation, we need to
know, precisely: (1) what the wind is, everywhere, and (2) exactly where
which wind turbines stand, and which model they are.

For historical wind, the ERA5 reanalysis is the standard choice.

For plant location and turbine type, the
Marktstammdatenregister (MaStR) is Germany’s own public register.

Alternatively, PECD (the Pan-European Climate Database) already does
a version of this, at a European scale, with more elaborate methodology
and proprietary inputs we don’t have access to.

records.content:
PECD v4.2’s wind capacity factor pipeline, in order:

Take ERA5 wind speed at 10m and 100m.

Apply a bias adjustment using Global Wind Atlas (GWA) data — ERA5’s
reanalysis wind speed is systematically off from observations in a
way that varies by location; GWA’s higher-resolution product corrects
this.

Extrapolate to each turbine’s actual hub height, using a
precomputed shear exponent (alpha) — wind speed doesn’t scale
linearly with height, alpha captures how steeply it changes.

Look up each location’s installed turbine type and compute a
capacity factor from that turbine’s power curve.

Correct for the wind farm’s actual layout — which turbines are in
the first row versus further back, since row position changes the wind
a turbine actually sees (wake effects).

Apply high-wind shutdown assumptions, per turbine.

records.content:
We rebuild this methodology with the means available to us: ERA5 for
weather (same source PECD itself uses), and MaStR for plant location
and turbine type (PECD uses a different, proprietary database —
WindPowerNet — that we don’t have access to).

The hard part is that there is no single ground-truth time series against
which to check whether the full replication is correct end to end. So
instead of one validation, we built a ladder of checks, each isolating
one step, each checked against whatever partial ground truth PECD itself
publishes:

Bias-adjusted wind speed vs. PECD’s own published bias-adjusted
wind speed grid — a genuine, direct ground truth, since PECD publishes
this as a gridded product in its own right.

Hub-height extrapolation — no direct ground truth exists (PECD
never publishes wind speed at arbitrary hub heights), so this is
instead checked for internal consistency: since alpha was itself
derived from the 10m/100m ratio, extrapolating our validated 100m field
back down to 10m via alpha should closely reproduce our validated 10m
field.

Zone-level capacity factor (PEON zones, the only spatial
aggregation PECD publishes for wind) vs. PECD’s own zone capacity
factors — comparable either as relative capacity factors, or, weighted
by MaStR’s installed capacity per zone, as absolute MW.

National aggregate — MaStR’s zone-level installed capacity lets us
weight the 7 PEON zones up to one Germany-wide number, comparable
against the same aggregation applied to PECD’s own zone figures (since
PECD itself publishes no ready-made national number for wind).

SMARD’s actual net wind generation — the one point of comparison
against real-world data, not just PECD’s own numbers. A deviation here
can come from two different sources that are easy to conflate: our
physical replication being imperfect, or curtailment/self-consumption
creating a genuine gap between gross physical generation and what
actually reaches the grid. Neither PECD’s product nor ours attempts to
model curtailment, so some gap here is expected even from a perfect
physical replication.

Three different ways of turning weather + MaStR capacity into a physically-
motivated wind feature have been built (see


Comparing all three approaches):

PECD’s own capacity factor, reweighted by MaStR capacity — trusts
PECD’s official numbers wholesale.

A simple from-scratch physics model (one generic turbine curve, raw
ERA5, no bias correction) — the simplest possible replication.

This project’s full replication — GWA-bias-adjusted wind speed,
alpha-based hub-height extrapolation, per-plant power curves matched to
real turbine models where possible.

None of these three is “the answer” in isolation — the actual target is
forecasting headline variables well, and any feature that helps with that
is worth keeping even where it deviates from PECD’s own methodology.
Replicating PECD as closely as possible is the validation exercise that
tells us how good a candidate feature is, not the end goal itself.

records.content:
Same ladder as onshore (per-plant power curves from MaStR, PECD’s alpha
grid for hub-height extrapolation, checked against PECD’s own zone product
then against SMARD’s actual wind_offshore generation), but two of
onshore’s steps needed a genuine methodology change rather than a
copy-paste, both found by checking intermediate results against real
numbers rather than assumed to transfer directly from onshore:

GWA2 barely covers the German offshore fleet. GWA’s own downscaling
(WAsP) explicitly excludes “offshore areas beyond 20 km” (per the PUG).
Checked against MaStR’s actual offshore turbine coordinates: 91% of
installed German offshore capacity sits at grid cells with no GWA2
delta-correction factor at all. Cross-checked against PECD’s own
downloaded bias-adjusted wind-speed product vs. raw ERA5 at those same
deep-sea cells: the ratio is ~1.0000 beyond ~20km from shore (real
correction only applies near-shore) — PECD’s own product evidently
leaves deep-offshore wind speed uncorrected too. The replication matches
that: apply the GWA delta where available, leave raw ERA5 speed
unmodified elsewhere.

The shared storm-shutdown model over-derates offshore. Its linear
ramp (20→25 m/s) is tuned against onshore, where hub-height wind speed
rarely exceeds 20 m/s; offshore it regularly does (checked: ~3.8% of
hours at a representative North Sea cell across 2022 fall in that 20-25
m/s band, vs. essentially never onshore). Applied as written it derated
a January storm snapshot to a third of PECD’s own product’s output at
that hour, even though the pre-shutdown power curve alone already
tracked PECD’s product closely (0.91 vs. 0.86) — same pattern as solar’s
inverter-loss polynomial: implemented elsewhere
(pecdr/shutdown.py), demonstrably doing net harm here, so left out of
the offshore chain with the discrepancy documented rather than patched
with an unvalidated offshore-specific threshold.

Offshore turbine technical detail in MaStR is markedly more complete than
onshore’s — 100% of active offshore capacity has a known turbine model
(vs. ~44-56% onshore) and 97.6% a known hub height — though only ~2.5% of
that capacity matches an exact public OEDB power curve (vs. ~44% onshore,
most offshore models being larger/newer than the library covers), so the
generic specific-power-parametrized fallback curve carries most of the
offshore fleet.

Against SMARD’s actual generation, this project’s replication reaches the
best correlation of the three (0.916, edging out even PECD’s own
official product’s 0.902) but with a larger absolute bias (+0.108 vs.
PECD’s +0.073 and the naive baseline’s +0.071) — it tracks the true
up-and-down weather pattern slightly better than PECD’s own product does,
but systematically overestimates the level more. Plausible drivers, none
isolated yet: German offshore wind has
well-documented real-world curtailment from delayed grid connections
(farms commissioned before their export cable is ready), which neither
this replication nor PECD’s own product attempts to model — the same
“no ground truth for curtailment” gap flagged for onshore above, likely
larger here since offshore grid-connection delays are a well-known,
material issue in the German market.

Is the bias just our own capacity accounting being wrong, rather than
curtailment? The “PECD official x MaStR” comparison above leans on this
project’s own MaStR-derived monthly PEOF-zone capacity panel for weighting
on both sides — so a wrong capacity vector could manufacture that same
bias with no real curtailment involved. Checked directly: solving for the
per-zone capacity vector that best reconstructs SMARD’s actual generation
from PECD’s own zone capacity-factor shapes (non-negative, monotonically
non-decreasing, via NNLS on a reparametrized design matrix — see notebook
35) drives the bias to roughly zero (-0.03 vs. MaStR weights’ +0.16 in MW
terms, same 3-zone basis), confirming a real chunk of the bias is
attributable to our own capacity numbers, not to PECD or curtailment.
But correlation barely moves (0.909 vs. 0.898) — reweighting capacity
fixes the level, not the shape. Since the fitted vector is by
construction the best any monotonic capacity story can do, that remaining
gap can’t be closed by better fleet data — it needs something the capacity
vector structurally can’t represent: curtailment or another dynamic
effect. The fitted national capacity trajectory is also strikingly
different in shape from MaStR’s: essentially flat 2020-2024 while
MaStR’s nameplate figure climbs steadily, only converging in 2025 — the
same window Germany’s offshore grid connections
(BorWin5/DolWin6-era converter platforms) were catching up with the
capacity build-out, consistent with, though not proof of, a growing
grid-bottleneck story.

One more data-quality finding along the way, worth flagging on its own:
3 of PECD’s 6 PEOF zones (DE013_OFF/DE014_OFF/DE015_OFF) are 100%
NaN in PECD’s own product across the entire 2015-2025 file — PECD
apparently never modeled them. DE013_OFF still carries real MaStR
capacity (up to ~300 MW), which was silently diluting the “PECD official x
MaStR” capacity-weighted denominator above with dead-weight capacity that
contributes nothing to the numerator — a small (~1.5-3% of national
capacity) but real effect, separate from the capacity-vector question
above. Fixed in notebook 34 by restricting that comparison to the zones
PECD actually has data for; the numbers already quoted throughout this
page reflect the fix. Removing the dilution moved “PECD official x MaStR”
bias up (+0.060 → +0.073), not down — the dilution had been partially
masking, not inflating, the true bias.

records.content:
Decompose horizontal irradiance (GHI) into beam and diffuse components
(Skartveit-Olseth, 1987).

Transpose onto the panel’s actual plane of array — Klucher’s (1979)
anisotropic sky model for diffuse sky radiation, plus a fixed-albedo
ground-reflected term.

Apply optical (reflection) losses at the panel surface (Martin-Ruiz).

Convert plane-of-array irradiance to module efficiency at 25°C via a
5-coefficient polynomial (Beyer et al., 2004), fit by PECD against real
German/French generation data.

Correct for cell temperature (Ross, 1976) and a linear thermal
derating coefficient.

Apply inverter losses via a 3-coefficient polynomial (Schmidt & Sauer,
1994).

A two-step temporal downscaling (hourly GHI/TA interpolated to
15-minute resolution, capacity factor computed at that finer step,
then averaged back to hourly) to better capture sunrise/sunset
variability.

records.content:
The wind and solar workstreams above check generation against SMARD.
The wider project goal, stated at the top of this page, is a day-ahead
residual-load forecast — which needs two things that are never directly
observed: gross power demand (grid-metered load plus invisible
behind-the-meter self-consumption) and renewable generation net of
curtailment. 

A walkthrough page teaches
this model start to finish — the problem, the mental model, the
equations, and the evidence, in that order — and a


dedicated reference page writes down
the full system of equations relating these hidden variables to what
this project can actually observe. This section summarizes what came out
of estimating them.

The gross-demand regression (notebook 38) fits grid-metered load as a
calendar/temperature demand model minus PV self-consumption, identified
by a simple structural fact: behind-the-meter self-consumption can only
exist when PV is producing, so nighttime and heavily overcast hours pin
down the demand-model coefficients with zero interference, while daytime
hours (where PV output varies a lot day to day from cloud cover, at fixed
calendar/weather conditions) pin down the self-consumption effect — one
regression, not two sequential models. Both of its built-in falsification
checks (a feed-in category that structurally cannot self-consume; wind
potential, which has no behind-the-meter channel at all) came back
significant rather than the expected zero — investigated rather than
brushed aside: the PV category split turned out to be a genuine
non-identification problem (the two candidate regressors correlate at
0.95), while wind’s effect survived a direct test of the obvious
alternative explanation (a richer temperature spline barely changed it)
and is more likely a real, different phenomenon — price-responsive
industrial demand rising during cheap, high-wind hours — that the test’s
own premise didn’t anticipate. The aggregate specification’s self-consumption
estimate (~12% of national PV potential, net of the ~40% of the fleet
that’s registered full-feed-in and structurally can’t self-consume at
all) is this notebook’s trustworthy headline number.

Curtailment estimation (notebook 39) calibrates a curtailment-rate-vs-
oversupply curve on wind’s own gap — clean because wind has no
behind-the-meter term to confound it — using a potential-based
oversupply proxy (P_total/D_true_hat, not the observed-generation-based
proxy from the wind-offshore workstream’s own bias-driver notebook, which
understates true oversupply exactly when curtailment is largest) and
transfers that curve to PV. The result reframes what’s driving PV’s gap
against SMARD: of its ~2177 MW average gap, ~1653 MW (76%) is predicted
curtailment — more than self-consumption, which wasn’t obvious going in.
The residual left over correlates with the self-consumption-registered
capacity share at 0.643, though both series simply trend upward together
over 2019-2025, so that number is suggestive rather than a tight
validated match.

The residual-load backtest (notebook 40), trained on 2019-2023 and
evaluated out-of-time on 2024-2025 against realized residual load
(computable directly from SMARD, no new data needed), shows the full
chain roughly halves the MAE of the naive baseline that skips all of
this hidden-variable estimation (4,856 MW vs. 10,560 MW) and cuts the bias
by roughly 5x (-1,936 MW vs. -9,750 MW), with a real but smaller
correlation improvement (0.915 vs. 0.905) — consistent with the demand and
curtailment corrections fixing the level more than the day-to-day
pattern, which both approaches already capture reasonably well from
shared weather inputs. (Caught and fixed while building this comparison:
the curtailment curve originally returned NaN for any out-of-time hour
whose oversupply proxy fell outside the training period’s own range —
4.1% of the test period — silently dropped rather than handled; fixed in
pecdr/residual_load.py by clipping into the fitted range, the same
graceful-degradation behavior a tree-based model gives for free.)

Does the structure actually earn its keep, though? (notebook 42)
splits “does weather information help” from “does explicitly modeling
unobserved quantities help on top of that,” with four more points on
the same out-of-time backtest: a calendar-only floor with no weather at
all, the same features as the full model fed into one flat linear
regression with no structural decomposition, the same features again fit
with LightGBM, and a capacity-factor-rescaled version of the LightGBM
model. The answers are not what a reader might expect: adding
raw weather-derived potential without correcting it for curtailment
(the naive baseline) is no better than no weather information at all in
absolute-error terms (10,560 MW MAE vs. 10,284 MW for calendar-only) —
correlation improves a lot (0.905 vs. 0.486) but the uncorrected bias
overwhelms that benefit. More surprisingly, a plain linear regression
given the same inputs as the full structural model, with none of the
hand-built equations, does better than the structural model on this
backtest (MAE 4,177 MW, corr 0.941, vs. the structural model’s 4,856 MW
/ 0.915) — in this setting, most of the benefit comes from having the
right features at all, not from the specific structural machinery used to
extract them. The LightGBM version underperforms the linear one, for a
concrete, checked reason rather than a mystery: installed capacity grew
throughout 2019-2025, so years_since_start has 100% of test-period rows
beyond the training range and P_wind_off_mw has 20% — tree-based models
cannot extrapolate a trend past what they were trained on, while a linear
trend term does so by construction.

Does capacity-factor rescaling fix LightGBM’s handicap, as expected?
Partially, not fully. A sixth model swaps P_i(t) for capacity factor
(P_i(t)/Capacity_i(t), bounded regardless of fleet size) as LightGBM’s
features and predicts ResidualLoad(t)/TotalCapacity(t) instead of MW
directly, reconstructing the final MW prediction by multiplying back by
the actual (looked-up, not modeled) capacity at the test time. This
narrows the gap substantially (MAE 6,714 → 5,294 MW) — confirming the
extrapolation story really was the mechanism — but doesn’t reach M3 or
even M2. Checked directly rather than left unexplained: the model’s error
in the normalized domain is tiny and essentially unbiased in-sample
(~0.000), but picks up a small out-of-sample bias (~0.006) on the test
period, and that small bias gets amplified when multiplied back by
TotalCapacity_mw to reconstruct MW — confirmed by a 0.44 correlation
between the signed MW error and total capacity at test time. Rescaling
fixes the tree’s input-side extrapolation problem; it trades in a
smaller, different amplification effect on the output-reconstruction
side instead.

records.content:
Residual load (demand minus renewable generation) drives prices, but
both halves of that subtraction are things we never directly observe:
gross power demand (grid-metered load, plus invisible
behind-the-meter self-consumption) and renewable generation net of
curtailment (what the weather could have produced, minus whatever grid
operators or market conditions stopped from reaching the grid). We only
ever see the already-contaminated versions of both.

Wind first, deliberately — not because it’s a clean match, but

This still is not apples-to-apples. The gap here is real and
substantial — it opens up specifically during the high-output stretches
where potential flattens out near the fleet’s ceiling, while observed
generation stays well below it. Wind has no behind-the-meter

what makes wind the clean calibration signal used below, not a
reassuring “these should match” chart.

PV’s version of the same chart mixes in a second effect:



Figure 2:Solar PV, Jun-Jul 2023: potential vs. observed (SMARD).

Every single day shows a gap at the peak, not just the high-oversupply
days the way wind did — consistent with self-consumption being a
constant companion to PV output, on top of the episodic curtailment
effect wind already showed. Separating those two is the rest of this
page.

Three checks worth knowing about, because they’re what earns trust in
the numbers above rather than just the numbers themselves:

Two built-in falsification checks, and both failed cleanly —
informatively, not fatally. A PV feed-in category that structurally
cannot self-consume should show a zero coefficient; it didn’t, and the
reason turned out to be that its regressor correlates at 0.95 with the
one that should show an effect, leaving too little independent
variation for plain OLS to separate them. Wind potential, which has no
self-consumption channel at all, also came back nonzero — but survived
a direct test of the obvious alternative explanation (a much richer
temperature response barely changed it), pointing instead at a real,
different phenomenon: price-responsive industrial demand rising during
cheap, high-wind hours. See 

notebook 38
for both in full.

Onshore and offshore wind were checked against each other
(

notebook 39) — both
structurally BTM-free, so if their curtailment-vs-oversupply shapes
diverged sharply, the “one shared curve” transfer to PV would be too
coarse. They agree from moderate oversupply upward, which is the range
that actually matters for PV’s own daylight hours.

The PV residual (curtailment already subtracted out) was checked
against an independent series: the self-consumption-registered
capacity share from MaStR, which the model never sees during fitting.
They correlate at 0.643 — supportive, though both simply trend upward
over 2019-2025, so treat this as suggestive rather than a tight
validated match.

Step 6 answers “is the full model better than doing nothing.” It doesn’t
answer a sharper question: does explicitly modeling the unobserved
quantities (D_true, the curtailment curve) beat simply handing the same
observed weather-derived features to a model and letting it find its
own answer?

Four findings here are worth sitting with, because none of them is the
“obviously expected” result:

M0 vs. M1: weather information, used carelessly, is not obviously
better than no weather information at all. M1 has much better
correlation than M0 (0.905 vs. 0.486 — it clearly tracks the pattern
better), but its uncorrected curtailment assumption produces a bias so
large that its absolute error ends up slightly worse than the
calendar-only floor’s.

M2 vs. M3: a plain linear regression, given the same inputs as the
full structural model but none of its equations, does better. Lower
MAE, higher correlation. The most likely reason: M2’s curtailment curve
is fit on wind and transferred to PV under a shared-curve assumption,
while M3’s regression fits PV’s own relationship to its own history
directly, with no transfer step to be wrong about.

M3 vs. M4: more flexibility didn’t help, for a specific, checked
reason, not a mysterious one. Installed capacity grew throughout
2019-2025, so years_since_start has 100% of test-period rows beyond
the training range and P_wind_off_mw has 20% — tree-based models
cannot extrapolate a trend past what they saw in training, while a
linear trend term does so by construction.

M4 vs. M5: rescaling by installed capacity helps, but doesn’t fully
fix it, and checking why turned up a second mechanism, not a dead end.
M5 (capacity factors as features, a capacity-normalized target,
rescaled back to MW by multiplying by the actual, looked-up capacity at
test time) cuts M4’s MAE from 6,714 to 5,294 MW — the extrapolation
story was real. But it still trails M3, because a different problem
takes its place: M5’s error in the normalized domain is tiny and
essentially zero in-sample, but picks up a small (~0.006) out-of-sample
bias on the test period — and multiplying that small bias back by
TotalCapacity_mw to reconstruct MW amplifies it, precisely because
capacity is largest late in the test period. Checked directly: the
signed MW error correlates with TotalCapacity_mw at 0.44. Rescaling
trades the tree’s input-side extrapolation problem for a smaller
output-side amplification problem — a real improvement, not a full fix.

So which is it — features, or structure? In this backtest, mostly
features: the biggest jump is M1→M2/M3 (weather-derived potential,
corrected for curtailment in some form), while M2→M3 shows the specific
hand-built structural form isn’t what’s earning that improvement, and a
simpler model given the same information does slightly better. That
doesn’t make the structural work wasted — it’s what made the
falsification checks, the wind/PV decomposition, and the equations page’s
account of why the gap exists possible, none of which a flat regression
can offer — but as a pure point-forecast for residual load, the more
complex approach needed to earn its keep here, and on this specific test,
it didn’t quite.

records.content:
The first checkpoint in replicating PECD v4.2’s wind methodology: can we
reproduce PECD’s Global Wind Atlas “Delta Adjustment” bias correction on
raw ERA5 wind speed, at two snapshot hours over Germany’s PEON extent?

No plant locations, power curves, or alpha extrapolation are involved yet
-- purely the bias-correction step in isolation, checked against ground
truth PECD itself publishes:

Inputs: our own raw ERA5 10m/100m wind speed
(pipeline/03_download_era5_wind_snapshots.py) and PECD’s own
ERA5/GWA2 climatology grids (pipeline/01_download_pecd_wind_bias_reference.py),
from which we recompute PECD’s Delta Adjustment factor ourselves
(pecdr/wind_bias.py).

Ground truth: PECD’s own published bias-corrected 10m/100m wind
speed grid (pipeline/02_download_pecd_wind_speed_snapshots.py) --
confirmed by inspection to genuinely be the post-correction product (its
own NetCDF history attribute records “Bias adjustment with mean delta
method” and “Removed drop at 10 UTC” as already-applied steps).

Not yet replicated (out of scope for this milestone -- see
pecdr/wind_bias.py): capping outliers above 70 m/s, and PECD’s ERA5
10:00 UTC dip interpolation. Neither snapshot hour is 10:00 UTC or a
storm event, so this shouldn’t matter yet.

Domain note: PECD’s ERA5/GWA2 climatology grids (used to derive the
Delta Adjustment factor) are NaN over sea cells -- they’re part of the
onshore-wind-specific bundle, so GWA2 coverage only exists over land.
PECD’s own published wind-speed product has no such gap (it’s a general
climate variable, valid over sea too). Comparisons below are restricted to
our own field’s non-NaN (onshore) footprint on both sides
(pecdr.wind_bias.restrict_to_onshore) so the two are compared over the
same domain.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import xarray as xr

from pecdr.domain import SNAPSHOT_TIMESTAMPS
from pecdr.paths import ProjPaths
from pecdr.pecd_io import open_single_zipped_netcdf
from pecdr.wind_bias import apply_delta_correction, delta_correction, raw_wind_speed, restrict_to_onshore, single_data_var

paths = ProjPaths()
paths.ensure_directories()

HEIGHTS_M = [10, 100]
SNAPSHOT_YEAR = "2020"
snapshot_times = pd.to_datetime(SNAPSHOT_TIMESTAMPS)

    v_hub = v100_at_plant * (plant_hub_height / 100) ** alpha_at_plant

    cf = plant_capacity_factor(v_hub, plants["matched_type"], plants["rated_wind_speed_ms"], curve_cache)
    cf = apply_shutdown_derate(cf, v_hub)
    cf = cf * (1 - OTHER_LOSSES_FRACTION)

capacity into a wind-onshore capacity factor, all developed across

records.content:
12_compare_all_approaches found that all three modeled series --
including PECD’s own official product (approach 1) -- systematically
overshoot SMARD’s actual wind-onshore generation at high capacity factors.
Since approach 1 isn’t derived from this project’s replication at all,
that shared pattern is evidence the gap is a genuine physical-vs-grid
effect (curtailment, high-wind shutdown, behind-the-meter
self-consumption -- see ../markdown/index.md), not a defect specific to
this project’s methodology.

This notebook digs into when the bias shows up, pooled across every
year in pecdr.domain.FULL_YEAR_BACKTEST_YEARS, to see which candidate
explanation it’s most consistent with:

Bias vs. CF level -- grows with output level, as expected if it’s
driven by high-wind curtailment/shutdown rather than a flat offset.

Bias vs. month -- larger in winter (higher wind and more grid
congestion) would point toward curtailment; a flat seasonal pattern
would point toward something structural instead (e.g. a fleet-vintage
or power-curve mismatch).

Bias vs. hour of day -- larger overnight, when demand is low and
negative prices make curtailment more likely, would support the
curtailment/oversupply story specifically (as opposed to shutdown,
which has no time-of-day preference of its own).

Bias vs. renewable oversupply -- (wind + solar) / load as a rough
proxy for how close the grid is to zero/negative residual load, the
condition curtailment is most likely under.

Bias vs. year -- checks whether any of the above is stable across
the backtest period, or whether one year is doing all the work.

records.content:
CF level and month: both patterns from the single-year (2020) pass
hold up over the full 2019-2025 backtest, and come out cleaner with 7x
the sample -- bias grows roughly monotonically with SMARD CF, and is
largest in the high-wind months (Jan/Feb, Oct-Dec), near zero in
summer. Both approaches (built from PECD’s official product and from
this project’s from-scratch replication respectively) show the same
shape, which is strong evidence the effect lives on the SMARD side of
the comparison -- wind-speed-driven curtailment and/or high-wind
shutdown -- not in either model.

Bias by year: stable at ~0.048-0.056 (approach 3) / ~0.014-0.017
(approach 1) for 2019-2022, then steps up to ~0.065-0.072 /
~0.015-0.023 for 2023-2025 -- both approaches step up together, at
the same point in time. That’s consistent with a real-world change
rather than a modeling artifact specific to either approach: Germany’s
reported wind curtailment volumes have risen substantially since
2022-2023 as grid congestion has worsened, which is exactly the
growing-curtailment trend this project’s own ../markdown/index.md
already flags as expected “to become more common, not less, as
renewable penetration grows.”

Hour of day: the sharp, localized dip around 10-11 UTC is not a
curtailment/oversupply signature after all -- it lines up exactly with
a documented ERA5 artifact already called out in this project’s own
pecdr/domain.py: “ERA5 has a documented spurious wind-speed dip at
[10:00 UTC], which PECD corrects via interpolation as a separate
preprocessing step not yet replicated here.” Approach 1 (PECD’s own
product, which does apply that correction) shows a much shallower dip
at the same hour than approach 3 (this project’s replication, which
doesn’t), consistent with this being substantially an uncorrected
input-data artifact in our pipeline rather than a distinct physical
effect. Concrete, fixable follow-up: interpolate across 10:00 UTC in
the raw ERA5 wind speed before running it through the rest of the
pipeline, the way PECD itself does.

Oversupply proxy: bias climbs with renewable share of load, but
this ratio is highly collinear with CF level itself (wind dominates the
numerator here), so this panel is largely a restatement of the first
result rather than independent evidence for oversupply-driven
curtailment specifically.

Net: the CF-level, seasonal, and year-over-year patterns all support
treating most of the remaining bias as wind-speed-driven curtailment/
shutdown that neither PECD’s own product nor this replication attempts
to model -- which is what makes a CF-conditional statistical
correction (e.g. quantile mapping, binned by CF level) a reasonable
next step for anyone consuming this as a forecasting feature. The
diurnal dip, on the other hand, looks like a specific, fixable
ERA5-interpolation gap rather than a modeling limitation to correct for
statistically.

overshoots SMARD’s actual wind-onshore CF in a way that grows roughly
monotonically with CF level, and recommended a CF-conditional statistical
correction as the practical next step rather than trying to model
curtailment mechanistically (no public ground truth exists to calibrate
a mechanistic model against -- see ../markdown/index.md).

This notebook fits that correction and tests it honestly: a monotonic
calibration curve (pecdr.bias_correction, isotonic regression of SMARD
CF on modeled CF) is fit on one calendar year only, then applied to
the next year -- never fit and evaluated on the same data. Walk
forward across the whole backtest period: train on 2019, correct 2020;
train on 2020, correct 2021; ... train on 2024, correct 2025. 2019 itself
is left uncorrected (no earlier year available in this project’s
backtest range) and serves as the uncorrected baseline.

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd

from pecdr.bias_correction import apply_correction, fit_isotonic_correction
from pecdr.capacity_weighting import total_hourly_capacity
from pecdr.domain import FULL_YEAR_BACKTEST_YEARS
from pecdr.paths import ProjPaths

paths = ProjPaths()
paths.ensure_directories()

TEST_YEARS = FULL_YEAR_BACKTEST_YEARS[1:]  # 2019 has no earlier year to train on

The correction is fit blind to the year it’s applied to (strictly
walk-forward, never fit-and-evaluate-on-the-same-year), so any
improvement reflects the bias’s known CF-conditional structure actually
generalizing one year ahead, not overfitting. Whether it does, and by how
much, is the print-out and the bias-by-year panel above -- read those
together with 22_analyse_bias_drivers’ finding that the bias itself
stepped up after 2022 rather than staying constant: a correction trained
on the year immediately before should adapt to that kind of slow drift
reasonably well (each year’s training data reflects last year’s
curtailment regime), but would lag a sudden, sharp regime change within
a single year.

The wind workstream’s structure, applied to solar for the first time:
two ways of turning weather + MaStR capacity into a PV capacity factor,
neither requiring any new physics work this round (see
pecdr/solar_technology.py and pipeline/24_build_solar_capacity_by_nuts2_month.py
for the newly-built piece: a crosswalk from MaStR’s own fields to PECD’s
4 PV technology codes, since MaStR doesn’t label units with them
directly).

PECD’s own NUTS2 x technology capacity factor x MaStR capacity by
technology -- trusts PECD’s official numbers wholesale, reweighted
by Germany’s actual installed capacity in each of PECD’s 4 PV
technology segments (60/61/62/63 = industrial rooftop / residential
rooftop / utility fixed / utility tracking).

This project’s existing simple physics baseline
(pecdr/physics.py’s solar_capacity_factor -- Erbs GHI
decomposition, one fixed tilt/azimuth for all of Germany, Faiman
cell temperature, PVWatts DC) -- no technology split, reweighted by
total installed capacity per NUTS2 zone regardless of technology.

Plus SMARD’s actual DE-LU PV generation as the real-world ground
truth neither approach is derived from.

Not attempted yet: a full per-plant physics replication using each
plant’s actual orientation/tilt (real data for this already exists in
MaStR’s solar_technical_detail, unlike PECD’s own assumed
tilt-distribution approach) -- a bigger undertaking, flagged as the
natural next phase once this first comparison is in.

import pandas as pd

from pecdr.capacity_weighting import capacity_weighted_cf, total_hourly_capacity
from pecdr.paths import ProjPaths

paths = ProjPaths()
paths.ensure_directories()

solar_capacity_month = pd.read_parquet(paths.solar_capacity_by_nuts2_month_file)

# Approach 1: PECD's own NUTS2 x technology CF x time-varying MaStR capacity,
# keyed on a flattened "technology_region" composite (e.g. "60_DE11") so the
# existing zone-capacity-weighting machinery (built for wind's single-key
# PEON zones) applies unchanged -- each technology-region pair is just
# another "zone" to weight and sum over.
pecd_solar_cf = pd.read_parquet(paths.pecd_solar_capacity_factors_file)
pecd_solar_cf.columns = [f"{tech}_{region}" for tech, region in pecd_solar_cf.columns]

tech_region_capacity = solar_capacity_month.copy()
tech_region_capacity["region_code"] = tech_region_capacity["pecd_technology"] + "_" + tech_region_capacity["nuts2_region"]
approach1 = capacity_weighted_cf(pecd_solar_cf, tech_region_capacity)

# Approach 2: this project's own simple physics baseline, technology-agnostic,
# weighted by total capacity per NUTS2 zone (summed across all 4 technologies).
own_solar_cf = pd.read_parquet(paths.own_solar_capacity_factors_file)
total_region_capacity = solar_capacity_month.groupby(["nuts2_region", "month"])["capacity_mw"].sum().reset_index()
total_region_capacity = total_region_capacity.rename(columns={"nuts2_region": "region_code"})
approach2 = capacity_weighted_cf(own_solar_cf, total_region_capacity)

# SMARD actual generation (MW) -> implied CF via time-varying total capacity
target_panel = pd.read_parquet(paths.target_panel_file)
total_capacity_hourly = total_hourly_capacity(total_region_capacity, target_panel.index)
smard_implied_cf = target_panel["pv"] / total_capacity_hourly

comparison = pd.DataFrame({
    "1_pecd_official_x_mastr": approach1,
    "2_own_physics_baseline": approach2,
    "3_smard_implied": smard_implied_cf,
}).dropna(how="all")
print(f"Hours with at least one series: {len(comparison):,}")
comparison.describe()

25_compare_solar_approaches found approach 1 (PECD official x
MaStR-by-technology capacity) tracks SMARD reasonably well overall
(corr=0.940, MAE=0.033) but with a small positive bias that grows over
the backtest period (2018: 0.006, 2025: 0.026). This notebook checks two
distinct candidate explanations, mirroring 22_analyse_bias_drivers’s
wind investigation but adapted for what’s actually different about
solar:

Curtailment, growing over time -- the same pattern found for wind,
where the bias stepped up after 2022-2023 alongside real, reported
increases in German curtailment. If solar shows the same CF-level and
year-over-year shape, that’s evidence for the same explanation.

Behind-the-meter self-consumption -- specific to solar: MaStR’s
pv_category shows ~44% of German solar capacity is
self-consumption (with or without storage), which SMARD’s net
grid-injected generation figure never sees (see ../markdown/index.md’s
“behind-the-meter blind spot”). Since our modeled series is a gross
capacity factor, periods/eras with a higher self-consumption capacity
share should show a larger gap if this is a real contributor -- a
check wind never needed, since wind has negligible self-consumption.
