The diurnal chart above was the real finding of this notebook, and it
doesn’t look like it belongs in the same “curtailment” story as wind’s:
testing a range of hour shifts between the model and SMARD series (not
shown here, done as a one-off check) found that PECD’s solar CF product
runs 1 hour ahead of true UTC -- shifting it back cuts MAE against
SMARD roughly in half (0.033 -> 0.016) and correlation rises from 0.940
to 0.982, consistently across every year, not just on average. The same
shift test on PECD’s wind product found no such improvement, so this
isn’t a bug in how this project reads PECD’s files (pecdr.pecd_io
handles both identically) -- it’s specific to PECD’s own solar product,
plausibly inherited from ERA5’s solar-radiation fields being
accumulated over the preceding hour while wind speed is instantaneous,
a labeling convention PECD’s solar product doesn’t appear to correct for.
Fixed at the source in pipeline/17_process_pecd_capacity_factors.py;
every number in this notebook and in 25_compare_solar_approaches
already reflects the correction.

With that artifact removed, what’s left is smaller and a genuinely
different shape than wind’s monotonic curtailment pattern: bias is
positive across most of the CF range but flips negative at the very
highest CF bins (clear-sky summer middays) -- the opposite direction
curtailment would push it. Not yet explained; a candidate worth checking
before assuming it’s physical is whether the monthly capacity snapshot
used for weighting lags Germany’s rapid recent solar build-out within
a given month, understating capacity (and so overstating CF) precisely
when a month’s true capacity was still rising toward its end.

The year-over-year growth in bias (2018: 0.006 -> 2025: 0.026) survives
the timestamp fix unchanged, and self-consumption share tracks it
closely too -- but self-consumption share has grown monotonically over
the same period, so this notebook can’t separate “more curtailment over
time” from “more self-consumption over time” from these two panels
alone. Both remain plausible, real, solar-specific contributors to
revisit once the per-plant physics replication (this workstream’s
still-open Phase B) gives an independent way to cross-check.

unit_panel = pd.read_parquet(paths.solar_unit_technology_file)

modeled_parts = []
for day in SELECTED_DAYS:
    day_ts = pd.Timestamp(day)
    month_str = f"{day_ts.year}-{day_ts.month:02d}"
    era5 = xr.open_dataset(paths.era5_month_file(month_str))
    day_era5 = era5.sel(time=slice(f"{day}T00:00", f"{day}T23:00"))
    # One extra leading hour, needed as an interpolation anchor by the
    # downscaled chain -- see solar_capacity_factor_for_config_downscaled.
    anchor_era5 = era5.sel(time=slice(f"{day_ts - pd.Timedelta(hours=1):%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M}", f"{day}T23:00"))

    ghi_grid = day_era5["surface_solar_radiation_downwards"] / 3600
    temp_grid = day_era5["2m_temperature"] - 273.15
    ghi_region = mask_weighted_regional_mean(ghi_grid, mask_de)
    temp_region = mask_weighted_regional_mean(temp_grid, mask_de)

    ghi_grid_anchor = anchor_era5["surface_solar_radiation_downwards"] / 3600
    temp_grid_anchor = anchor_era5["2m_temperature"] - 273.15
    ghi_region_anchor = mask_weighted_regional_mean(ghi_grid_anchor, mask_de)
    temp_region_anchor = mask_weighted_regional_mean(temp_grid_anchor, mask_de)
    era5.close()

    is_active = (unit_panel["commissioning_date"] <= day_ts) & (unit_panel["final_shutdown_date"].isna() | (unit_panel["final_shutdown_date"] > day_ts))
    configs = expand_orientation(unit_panel.loc[is_active])
    configs = configs[configs["capacity_mw"] > 0]
    print(f"{day}: {len(configs):,} (region, technology, orientation) configs, {configs['capacity_mw'].sum():,.0f} MW total")

    for (region, tech), group in configs.groupby(["nuts2_region", "pecd_technology"], observed=True):
        if region not in ghi_region.columns:
            continue
        total_capacity = group["capacity_mw"].sum()
        weighted_cf = pd.Series(0.0, index=ghi_region.index)
        weighted_cf_downscaled = pd.Series(0.0, index=ghi_region.index)
        lat, lon = centroids.loc[region, "lat"], centroids.loc[region, "lon"]
        for row in group.itertuples():
            cf = solar_capacity_factor_for_config(
                ghi_region[region], temp_region[region],
                lat=lat, lon=lon,
                tilt_deg=row.tilt_deg, azimuth_deg=row.azimuth_deg, is_tracked=row.is_tracked,
            )
            cf_downscaled = solar_capacity_factor_for_config_downscaled(
                ghi_region_anchor[region], temp_region_anchor[region],
                lat=lat, lon=lon,
                tilt_deg=row.tilt_deg, azimuth_deg=row.azimuth_deg, is_tracked=row.is_tracked,
            )
            weighted_cf = weighted_cf + cf * row.capacity_mw
            weighted_cf_downscaled = weighted_cf_downscaled + cf_downscaled * row.capacity_mw
        weighted_cf = weighted_cf / total_capacity
        weighted_cf_downscaled = weighted_cf_downscaled / total_capacity
        modeled_parts.append(pd.DataFrame({
            "timestamp": weighted_cf.index,
            "modeled_cf": weighted_cf.to_numpy(),
            "modeled_cf_downscaled": weighted_cf_downscaled.to_numpy(),
            "nuts2_region": region,
            "pecd_technology": tech,
        }))

modeled = pd.concat(modeled_parts, ignore_index=True)

PECD’s documented “two-step temporal downscaling” was the other open
candidate for this gap. Its first step (3-hourly -> hourly, via a
clearness-index conversion) only applies to the climate-projections
stream -- this project’s ERA5 source is already hourly, so it’s not
applicable here. Its second step -- hourly GHI/TA interpolated to
15-minute resolution, CF computed at that finer step, then averaged
back to hourly, applicable to “both historical and projected datasets”
per the PUG -- was implemented (pecdr/temporal_downscaling.py) and run
side by side with the plain-hourly chain above.

Essentially no change, and per-technology it’s a wash to very slightly
worse across all four (see stats_by_tech above). It also doesn’t fix
the near-0-PECD-CF overshoot cluster that motivated trying it: in that
specific band (PECD CF < 0.02, hourly-modeled CF > 0.05, n=227), mean
modeled CF rises from 0.110 to 0.121 with downscaling -- moving
further from, not closer to, PECD’s near-zero readings.

One implementation pitfall worth flagging for anyone revisiting this:
the first version of this downscaling divided GHI by TOA irradiance
sampled instantaneously at each hourly timestamp to build the
clearness index -- but ERA5’s hourly GHI is a backward-looking mean
over the preceding hour. Whenever apparent sunset fell inside that
hour but before its end (e.g. DE30, 2020-01-15, the hour ending 16:00:
mean GHI 1.5 W/m2, but instantaneous TOA exactly 0 at 16:00), the
instantaneous-TOA denominator was 0 and the entire hour’s reconstructed
GHI was spuriously zeroed. That version made the match against PECD
markedly worse (corr 0.930 -> 0.883). Averaging TOA over the same
(t-1h, t] window as the GHI value it divides -- matching conventions
instead of mixing an instantaneous sample with an hourly mean --
resolved the artifact and produced the neutral result above.

So: this replication’s ~0.930 correlation ceiling isn’t explained by
missing temporal downscaling. The inverter-loss discrepancy (previous
section) remains the one open documented-but-unreconciled piece of the
chain, and is the more likely place to look next -- alongside anything
not documented in the PUG at all.

The new chain is a real, consistent improvement over the original
simple baseline -- lower bias, lower MAE, higher correlation, in
every single year 2019-2025 (see yearly_stats above), not just on
average. Matching PECD’s own product more closely (pipeline/27: corr
0.934 on 3 selected days) turns out to also mean matching reality more
closely, at least directionally -- that wasn’t guaranteed going in,
since the two claims (matching PECD vs. matching SMARD) are logically
separate.

But PECD’s own official product remains substantially closer to
SMARD than either of this project’s own-physics approaches -- roughly
a 3x smaller MAE and a much tighter scatter (see the 3-panel comparison
above). PECD’s pipeline evidently includes calibration against real
generation data and/or loss terms this replication doesn’t have or
couldn’t reconcile (the still-unresolved inverter-loss step from
pipeline/27, most likely, plus whatever else isn’t documented in the
PUG at all).

The new chain systematically over-predicts, and the over-prediction
grows sharply with output level, saturating around a +0.08-0.09 CF
bias above roughly 30% capacity factor (see the bias-vs-level chart).
Two standing candidates, neither newly ruled in or out by this
full-year run: the documented inverter-loss polynomial (pipeline/27
found it makes the match against PECD’s own product worse when
applied as written, so it’s currently omitted -- but omitting it may
just be trading one bias for another when compared against real
generation instead of PECD’s product), and unmodeled self-consumption
(rooftop generation consumed behind the meter never reaches SMARD’s
measured feed-in, and disproportionately so during high-output hours --
the same hypothesis pipeline/26_analyse_solar_bias_drivers.py explored
for the original baseline).

All three approaches’ error vs. SMARD grows worse year over year
(PECD’s own bias: 0.0001 in 2020 -> 0.026 in 2025; this project’s new
chain: 0.024 -> 0.046) -- including PECD’s own official product, which
isn’t affected by any modeling choice this project makes. That points
to something external to all three physics chains: growing
self-consumption share, unmodeled degradation, or a shifting technology
mix not fully captured by MaStR’s own classification -- worth its own
investigation before trusting any of these approaches for recent years
specifically.

records.content:
Same chain as the onshore replication
(09_replicate_wind_onshore_capacity_factor): bias-corrected 100m wind
speed -> hub-height extrapolation via PECD’s own alpha grid -> per-plant
power curve -> simplified probabilistic storm-shutoff derate -> flat 10%
“other losses” derate -> capacity-weighted aggregation to PEOF zone ->
compared against PECD’s own published PEOF zone capacity factor.

One deliberate difference from onshore: GWA2, PECD’s own bias-correction
reference, excludes “offshore areas beyond 20 km” (per the PUG). Checked
empirically against MaStR’s actual offshore turbine coordinates: 91% of
installed German offshore capacity sits at grid cells with no GWA2
delta factor at all. Cross-checked against PECD’s own downloaded
bias-adjusted wind-speed snapshot vs. raw ERA5 at those same deep-sea
cells: the ratio is ~1.0000 beyond ~20km from shore (real correction only
applies near-shore) -- i.e. PECD’s own product evidently leaves
deep-offshore wind speed uncorrected. pecdr.wind_bias.apply_delta_correction’s
fill_value=1.0 replicates that: apply the GWA delta where available,
leave raw ERA5 speed unmodified elsewhere.

Ground truth comes straight from pecd_wind_offshore_capacity_factors_file
(pipeline/17’s multi-year processed PEOF product) rather than a dedicated
snapshot-only download -- it already covers both snapshot hours (both in
2020), unlike onshore’s PEON ground truth, which needed its own
pipeline/07 download.

Same simplifications as onshore, except one: pecdr.shutdown’s
storm-shutdown ramp (linear derate 20->25 m/s) is not applied here.
It’s tuned against the onshore fleet, where hub-height wind speed rarely
exceeds 20 m/s; offshore it regularly does (checked: ~3.8% of hours at a
representative North Sea cell across 2022 fall in that 20-25 m/s band,
vs. essentially never onshore). Applied as-is it derates the January
snapshot below by ~75% at a moment PECD’s own product stays near full
output -- the pre-shutdown power curve alone already tracks PECD’s
product closely there (0.91 vs. PECD’s 0.86), so the ramp is doing net
harm, not good, exactly like the solar inverter-loss polynomial
(pecdr/solar_config_physics.py’s INVERTER_COEFS): implemented
elsewhere, deliberately not applied here, discrepancy left visible rather
than silently patched with an unvalidated offshore-specific threshold.

Same comparison as onshore’s 12_compare_all_approaches, adapted to three
approaches (there’s no offshore equivalent of the delu-headline-forecast
sibling project’s baseline to reuse as a fourth):

PECD’s own PEOF zone capacity factor x MaStR zone capacity --
trusts PECD’s official numbers wholesale, just reweights them by
MaStR’s installed capacity.

This project’s own naive physics baseline (pipeline/20) --
computed from scratch with the simplest possible physics: one generic
turbine power curve for the entire fleet, raw ERA5, no bias
correction. This is the “without PECD data” replication.

This project’s PECD replication (pipeline/30-32) -- computed
from scratch with PECD’s actual documented methodology as closely as
achievable: GWA2 bias-adjusted wind speed where available (else raw
ERA5 -- see 31’s docstring), alpha-based hub-height extrapolation,
per-plant power curves. No storm-shutdown derate (see 31/32’s
docstrings for why).

records.content:
Solve SMARD_actual_MW(t) ~ sum_z w_z(t) * PECD_CF_z(t) for the
per-zone capacity weights w_z(t), via ordinary least squares with two
physical constraints: w_z(t) >= 0, and w_z monotonically
non-decreasing in t (no German offshore capacity was decommissioned in
2019-2025, only added). The monotonicity constraint turns into a plain
non-negativity constraint via a reparametrization: instead of estimating
w_z(t) directly, estimate non-negative monthly increments
d_z[m] >= 0 (capacity newly delivering in zone z, month m -- the
first month’s increment absorbs whatever was already installed before the
fit window starts), so w_z(t) = sum_{k <= month(t)} d_z[k] is
automatically monotonic. Substituting back in, the model is linear again
in d, solved with plain NNLS (scipy.optimize.nnls) on a transformed
design matrix: column (z, k) at hour t is PECD_CF_z(t) if
month(t) >= k, else 0.

notebook’s “PECD official x MaStR” number silently dilutes its
capacity-weighted denominator with this dead-weight capacity (MaStR
capacity that contributes zero numerator, since its CF is NaN and
pandas’ default skipna sum just drops it). Only the 3 zones PECD
actually models (DE011_OFF, DE012_OFF, DE02_OFF) can be fit or
fairly compared here.

the design matrix is poorly conditioned for separating individual
zone weights -- capacity can trade between DE011_OFF and DE012_OFF

CF level: hump-shaped, not monotonic like onshore’s. Bias climbs
from ~0 up to a peak around CF~0.5 (+0.13 to +0.22), then falls back
toward zero (even slightly negative for approach 1) at the highest CF
bins (0.8-0.9) -- unlike onshore, where bias grows roughly monotonically
all the way to the top. Two plausible, non-exclusive drivers: PECD’s own
product (approach 1) does apply a per-turbine storm-shutdown model in
its own methodology (unlike this project’s replication, which dropped
it -- see 31’s docstring), which would pull approach 1 down at extreme
wind specifically; and this project’s own capacity estimate carries real
uncertainty in exactly the direction that would produce this shape (see
35 -- a capacity underestimate at a given hour inflates
SMARD_MW / our_capacity right into the highest bins). Both approaches
share the reversal, though, which favors something structural over an
artifact specific to one methodology -- not fully resolved here.

Month: consistent with the curtailment/oversupply story, same
direction as onshore -- bias is largest in winter (Jan/Feb, Oct-Dec,
+0.10 to +0.14) and smallest in summer (Jun-Aug), though unlike onshore
it never approaches zero even in summer (+0.055 at the lowest), tracking
offshore’s consistently higher year-round wind resource.

Hour of day: the opposite of the naive expectation, and different
from onshore. Bias peaks at midday (9-13 UTC, when demand and prices
are typically highest) and is lowest overnight (00-05 UTC) -- the
reverse of “curtailment happens overnight when demand is low.” The same
ERA5 10:00 UTC artifact already identified for onshore
(pecdr/domain.py) shows up again here, as a small dip in approach 3
only (approach 3 has no correction for it; approach 1, built from PECD’s
own corrected product, doesn’t show it) -- consistent cross-validation
of that already-identified, fixable gap, not new evidence either way for
curtailment. The midday peak itself is more consistent with solar PV
compounding total system oversupply at the same hours offshore wind is
already contributing a lot, than with offshore wind curtailment being
driven by its own local conditions alone.

Oversupply proxy: the cleanest, most monotonic result of the five,
and a stronger signal than onshore’s own version of this check. Bias
climbs steadily with (PV + wind onshore + wind offshore) / load, all
the way to the highest bin (+0.23 to +0.27) -- no reversal at the top,
unlike the CF-level panel. Onshore’s equivalent panel was flagged as
“largely a restatement” of CF level, since the two are highly collinear
there; here they behave genuinely differently (CF-level reverses at the
top, this doesn’t), which is more consistent with a real, at least
partially independent, system-wide oversupply effect than with
offshore’s own wind level alone.

Year: bias roughly doubles from a 2019-2021 baseline (+0.05 to +0.08)
to a 2023-2024 peak (+0.10 to +0.14), then eases in 2025 (+0.09 to
+0.12) -- independently corroborating two other findings already in
this project: 34’s yearly bias table (same shape) and 35’s fitted
national capacity trajectory (flat 2020-2024, only converging with
MaStR’s nameplate figure in 2025). Matches the real-world timeline of
Germany’s offshore grid-connection build-out (BorWin5/DolWin6-era
platforms) catching up with capacity additions.

Net: three independent diagnostics in this project now (this notebook’s
year and oversupply panels, and 35’s capacity-fitting exercise) converge
on the same time-varying, system-wide-oversupply-linked story, which is
more convincing pooled than any single one of them alone. The CF-level
reversal and the midday-peaked diurnal pattern are the two genuinely
offshore-specific departures from onshore’s equivalent findings -- both
have plausible explanations (storm-shutdown/capacity-ceiling effects at
extreme CF; solar-compounded midday oversupply) but neither is nailed
down without real curtailment or price data, the natural next step this
notebook doesn’t attempt.

Fits equation 7/7a from book/markdown/curtailment_system_equations.md:
grid-metered load (D_grid) as a calendar + temperature demand model,
minus PV self-consumption, split by MaStR feed-in category. The
identification argument: at hours with P_pv(t)=0 (night, heavily
overcast), the self-consumption terms vanish and the demand-model
coefficients are pinned down with no solar interference at all; daytime
hours, where P_pv(t) varies a lot day to day at fixed calendar/weather
conditions (cloud cover), then pin down the self-consumption
coefficients. One regression, not two sequential models.

Two falsification checks follow directly from the model’s own structure,
not from any external data:

P_pv,full_feed_in’s coefficient should be statistically
indistinguishable from zero -- that capacity is barred from
self-consuming by its own feed-in registration.

Adding wind potential terms to the same regression should also come
back ≈0 -- wind has no behind-the-meter self-consumption to detect.

    "+ P_pv_full_feed_in_mw + P_pv_self_consumption_mw + P_wind_on_mw + P_wind_off_mw"

assumed-zero coefficient rests on “no behind-the-meter self-consumption
channel,” but there’s a different, entirely legitimate channel wind
does have that solar’s full-feed-in category doesn’t need either --
high wind tends to push wholesale prices down, and some
price-responsive industrial demand (aluminium smelting and similar) is
known to ramp up during cheap/high-renewable hours. That’s a real
demand-side response, not a self-consumption artifact, and this
regression was never designed to net it out. It’s also a plausible
partial confound for the PV self-consumption estimate above, in the
opposite direction (if solar has a similar price effect, it should
push the PV coefficient toward positive/less-negative, not more
negative) -- so the aggregate self-consumption fraction reported above
is a reasonable estimate, but likely a slight underestimate of true
self-consumption if this channel is real, not an overestimate.

informative than a clean pass would have been. The full-feed-in/

dropped.

Wind’s nonzero coefficient survived a direct test of the obvious
alternative explanation (temperature misspecification leaking through
a correlate of wind) and is more likely a real, different effect this
falsification check’s own premise didn’t anticipate: price-responsive
industrial demand rising during cheap, high-wind hours. That’s a
legitimate demand-side phenomenon, not an artifact -- but it’s also a
plausible reason the PV self-consumption estimate above is a slight
underestimate, if a similar (opposite-signed) price effect exists for
solar.

The temperature response has the expected V-shape on the heating
side, and an essentially flat, insignificant cooling side -- plausibly
real (Germany’s historically low air-conditioning penetration), not
a red flag.

D_true_hat visibly fills in the summer midday dip that D_grid
shows (the intraday-profile chart) -- the gap between the two peaks at
9-17 UTC specifically, exactly where solar output is highest. In
winter the gap is much smaller and roughly flat across the whole day
rather than midday-concentrated -- consistent with it being mostly
ordinary model-fit residual (R²=0.84, not 1.0) rather than a solar
effect, since there’s little sun to self-consume in winter in the
first place.

above) is this notebook’s headline number, with two honestly-reported
caveats (the category split, and the wind confound) rather than a single
clean result. Both curtailment estimation (39) and the residual-load

Fits equations 9-10a from book/markdown/curtailment_system_equations.md.
Wind’s own gap (P_i(t) - G_i(t)) has no behind-the-meter term to
separate out -- it’s L_repair + L_price + L_congestion + ε directly, a
clean signal for how curtailment responds to system-wide oversupply.
That relationship, fit on wind, is then applied to PV’s own oversupply
hours; what’s left over in PV’s gap after subtracting the predicted
curtailment is an estimate of PV’s self-consumption plus its own repair
losses and model error.

Curtailment is expressed as a rate relative to each technology’s own
potential (Gap_i(t) / P_i(t)), not an absolute MW level, before
transferring the wind-fitted relationship to PV -- wind and PV have very
different capacity scales, so only a fraction of potential lost is
meaningfully comparable across technologies experiencing the same
system-wide oversupply conditions.

The oversupply proxy used here is the potential-based one (equation
9: P_total(t) / D_true_hat(t)), not the observed one from notebooks
22/36 -- the observed version is built from already-curtailed values, so
it understates true oversupply exactly when curtailment is largest.

Onshore and offshore agree reasonably well from oversupply~0.6
upward -- the region that matters most for transferring the curve to
PV, since PV’s own oversupply hours (daylight, when PV itself
contributes to the numerator) skew toward this range. Below that,
offshore’s rate goes sharply negative (as low as -0.7) while onshore
stays mildly positive -- a real divergence, not smoothed over here, most
plausibly a residual imperfection in the offshore replication at low
wind speeds (this project’s own offshore chain is the newer, less
independently cross-checked of the two) rather than evidence the
shared-curve assumption is wrong where it’s actually used.

The wind-calibrated curve explains most of PV’s raw gap: of the
~2177 MW average gap, ~1605 MW (74%) is predicted curtailment, leaving
a ~519 MW residual for self-consumption + repair + model error --
curtailment, not self-consumption, is the larger piece of PV’s own
gap, which wasn’t obvious going in.

The residual correlates with the self-consumption-registered capacity
share at 0.643 -- supportive, but both series simply trend upward
over 2019-2025, so part of this is two trending series moving together
rather than tight month-to-month co-movement. Worth a follow-up
detrended check (year-over-year differences instead of levels) before
leaning on this number heavily.

Fits equation 11 from book/markdown/curtailment_system_equations.md:
ResidualLoad_hat(t) = D_true_hat(t) - (P_total(t) - L_hat(t)) -- built
entirely from calendar + weather (D_true_hat, P_total) and the
wind-calibrated curtailment curve (L_hat, notebook 39), so everything
on the right-hand side is knowable ahead of a day-ahead forecast.

Trained on 2019-2023, evaluated out-of-time on 2024-2025 -- against the
one target this project can check without any new data: realized
residual load, D_grid(t) - sum_i G_i(t), computable directly from SMARD
for the whole backtest period. Compared against the naive baseline of
skipping the whole hidden-variable exercise (raw calendar-fit D_grid,
raw P_total with no curtailment correction) -- matching this project’s
established habit of always checking whether added complexity earns its
keep (done for every other workstream here: wind onshore, wind offshore,
solar).

One honest limit on what this backtest can prove, from notebook 38’s own
findings: since behind-the-meter self-consumption cancels out of residual
load by construction, a good fit here validates the net effect of the
whole chain, not that every individual hidden variable (k, L_hat) was
separately estimated correctly -- see notebook 38’s falsification checks
for that.

40_forecast_residual_load compared two points: a naive baseline (no
self-consumption or curtailment correction) and the full structural model
(equations 7-11, explicitly estimating the hidden D_true and L_hat).
That comparison conflates two separate questions: does having
weather-derived information at all help, and does how it’s used (flat
features vs. explicitly modeling unobserved quantities) matter on top of
that? This notebook adds three more points to separate them:

M0 -- calendar only, no weather at all. The true “zero weather
information” floor: predicts residual load directly from day of week,
hour, holiday, and a year trend. Even the naive baseline from 40
already uses weather-derived wind/solar potential on the supply side,
so it doesn’t answer “does weather help at all” on its own.

M3 -- the same weather + potential-generation features as the full
model, but no structure at all. One flat linear regression predicting
observed residual load directly from calendar, temperature, and
P_wind_on/P_wind_off/P_pv -- no separate demand/supply estimation,
no D_true vs. D_grid distinction, no curtailment curve.

M4 -- the same features as M3, fit with LightGBM instead of a linear
model -- tests whether a flexible, nonlinear model closes the gap to
the structural model without any hand-built equations at all.

All five models share the same train/test split (2019-2023 / 2024-2025)
and the same target: realized residual load, computed directly from
SMARD, never estimated.

    NAIVE_DEMAND_FORMULA,
    WEATHER_AND_POTENTIAL_RHS,
    curtailment_rate,
    fit_curtailment_curve,
    predict_curtailment_mw,
)

demand_model = smf.ols(AGGREGATE_DEMAND_FORMULA, data=train).fit()


def d_true_hat_of(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Series:
    return demand_model.predict(df.assign(P_pv_mw=0.0))


p_total_train = train["P_wind_on_mw"] + train["P_wind_off_mw"] + train["P_pv_mw"]
oversupply_train = p_total_train / d_true_hat_of(train)

min_potential_on = 0.05 * train["P_wind_on_mw"].max()
min_potential_off = 0.05 * train["P_wind_off_mw"].max()
p_wind_total_train = train["P_wind_on_mw"].where(train["P_wind_on_mw"] > min_potential_on, 0) + train["P_wind_off_mw"].where(
    train["P_wind_off_mw"] > min_potential_off, 0
)
gap_wind_total_train = (train["P_wind_on_mw"] - target_train["wind_onshore"]).where(train["P_wind_on_mw"] > min_potential_on, 0) + (
    train["P_wind_off_mw"] - target_train["wind_offshore"]
).where(train["P_wind_off_mw"] > min_potential_off, 0)
rate_wind_train = (gap_wind_total_train / p_wind_total_train).where(p_wind_total_train > 0)

installed renewable capacity, rather than residual load in MW directly.

learns the weather-driven pattern in the normalized quantity; the actual
MW prediction is reconstructed afterward by multiplying back by
TotalCapacity_mw, which is simply looked up at the target time, not

records.content:
The natural fix for M4’s extrapolation problem: stop feeding the tree a
trending absolute-MW target and trending absolute-MW features at all.
M5 uses capacity factors (CF_i(t) = P_i(t)/Capacity_i(t), bounded
~0-1 regardless of fleet size) as features and predicts
ResidualLoad(t)/TotalCapacity(t) as the target, reconstructing MW
afterward by multiplying back by the actual (looked-up, not modeled)
capacity at the test time.

This does help -- M5’s MAE (5,294 MW) is meaningfully better than
M4’s (6,714 MW), confirming the extrapolation story above was real and
that removing the trend from the tree’s own inputs matters. But it
doesn’t fully close the gap to M3, and checking why turns up a second,
different mechanism rather than “the fix didn’t work”: M5’s error in
the normalized domain is tiny and nearly unbiased in-sample (bias
~0.000 on training data), but picks up a small out-of-sample bias
(~0.006) on the test period -- and that small normalized-domain bias
gets amplified when multiplied back by TotalCapacity_mw to
reconstruct MW, precisely because capacity is largest in exactly the
(later) part of the test period. Checked directly: the signed MW error
correlates with TotalCapacity_mw at 0.44. Rescaling fixes the tree’s
input-side extrapolation problem; it introduces a smaller, different
error-amplification effect on the output-reconstruction side instead.

records.content:
Read the gaps between adjacent bars, not just the bars themselves --
each comparison isolates one specific question:

M0 vs. M1: does weather information help at all? Surprisingly,
M1 (naive baseline, using temperature and raw weather-derived
potential) has a higher MAE than M0 (calendar only, no weather at
all) -- 10,560 MW vs. 10,284 MW -- despite much better correlation
(0.905 vs. 0.486). Weather information clearly helps track the
pattern, but M1’s total disregard for curtailment produces such a
large systematic bias (-9,750 MW) that it overwhelms that benefit in
absolute-error terms. Weather data alone, used carelessly, is not
obviously better than no weather data at all.

M1 vs. M2/M3: does correcting for curtailment/self-consumption (in
some form) help once weather is already in the model? Emphatically
yes -- both M2 and M3 roughly halve M1’s MAE and cut its bias by
4-5x, by accounting for the fact that not all potential reaches the
grid.

M2 vs. M3: does the specific structural form (equations 7-11) beat
a plain linear regression given the same inputs? Here, no --
M3 (MAE 4,177, corr 0.941) beats M2 (MAE 4,856, corr 0.915). A flat
regression, free to learn its own best-fit relationship between P_i
and residual load, does better than the hand-built decomposition in
this backtest. Plausible reason: M2’s curtailment curve is calibrated
on wind and transferred to PV under a shared-curve assumption (see
notebook 39’s own robustness check on that assumption); M3’s
regression instead fits PV’s relationship to its own history directly,
with no transfer involved.

M3 vs. M4 vs. M5: does a flexible nonlinear model help further,
given the same information? Not in this setup. M4 underperforms M3
for the tree-extrapolation reason above; M5’s capacity-factor
rescaling measurably narrows that gap (MAE 6,714 -> 5,294 MW) without
closing it, for the amplification reason just checked. Neither
flexible-model variant beats the plain linear regression here.

Net answer to the original question: in this backtest, the
improvement over the naive baseline comes mostly from having the
weather-derived potential-generation features at all, not from the
specific structural machinery built to extract unobserved quantities --
a plain linear regression on the same inputs did the best of all six.
That’s a real result, not a foregone conclusion, and it doesn’t mean the
structural approach was wasted effort: it’s what made the falsification
checks, the wind/PV decomposition, and the equations-page account of
why the gap exists possible in the first place -- M3 has no equivalent
explanation for its own coefficients. But as a pure point-forecast for
residual load specifically, it’s the more complex approach that needed
to earn its keep here, and on this test it didn’t.

Wind dominates curtailment volume, and offshore is curtailed far
more heavily relative to its fleet size than onshore -- a real,
measured asymmetry this project’s model doesn’t currently distinguish
(the curtailment curve in notebooks 39/40/42 is calibrated on pooled
onshore+offshore wind, then transferred to PV as well).

PV curtailment is real but smaller in absolute terms, and clearly
seasonal, peaking alongside PV’s own generation season rather than at
some independent time.

This is a lower bound on total curtailment, not the whole picture:
it only captures grid-operator-ordered redispatch, not market-based
(negative-price) curtailment, which this data source doesn’t report at
all.

The natural next question -- does this real data actually support the
wind-to-PV curve-transfer assumption used in the residual-load model,
or does it call for a PV-specific curve -- is deliberately left open
here; this chapter’s only job was building a feel for the data itself.
